=== TSSA Comments on SERVM and CONE Assumptions FINAL.pdf ===
                                     PROJECT NO. 58777

 TRIENNIAL RELIABILITY                           §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 ASSESSMENT FOR THE ERCOT                        §
 REGION UNDER §25.508                            §                   OF TEXAS

               TEXAS SOLAR + STORAGE ASSOCIATION COMMENTS
              ON PROPOSED SERVM INPUT AND CONE ASSUMPTIONS


       The Texas Solar + Storage Association files these comments in response to the questions

filed by the Staff of the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Staff) in this project on January 30,

2026, regarding the SERVM input and CONE assumptions proposed by ERCOT.

       The Texas Solar + Storage Association (TSSA) is the statewide association dedicated to

the expansion of solar power and energy storage technologies in Texas. Our member companies

are engaged in the development, installation, and operations of utility-scale, industrial,

commercial, and residential solar and energy storage facilities and products, serving wholesale and

retail customers with predictable, affordable, clean power. Since 2014, TSSA has advocated on

behalf of its members before the Texas Legislature, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT

or Commission), as well as ERCOT. Our members have installed roughly two-thirds of the solar

and storage capacity in ERCOT and represent a large portion of the project development queue.

                                 I. GENERAL COMMENTS

       TSSA appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the inputs and assumptions

proposed by ERCOT for use in the probabilistic reliability assessment required by 16 TAC

§25.508(c). The results of this reliability assessment are largely dependent upon the assumptions

and forecasts used in the model, many of which have significant uncertainty, particularly for the

2029 study year. If the assessment demonstrates that the ERCOT market is not meeting the

reliability standard, the Commission will consider market design changes that could potentially


                                                1
 improve the reliability of ERCOT bulk power system based upon these assessment results. Given

the great uncertainty associated with some of the modeling assumptions, as well as the resulting

costs on customers and market impacts of any potential market design changes, TSSA recommends

that the Commission carefully consider and evaluate multiple scenarios and sensitivities associated

with key reliability assessment assumptions, particularly for the 2029 study year. The Commission

could then consider the costs of various proposals to meet any identified deficiency under a base

case scenario, as well as under sensitivity cases. This will help inform the Commission and the

public when weighing the potential costs and benefits associated with any market design changes,

if needed. Requiring ERCOT to run sensitivity analyses in addition to the base case recognizes

that the modeling results are dependent upon highly uncertain inputs and have a range of outcomes

that could occur under alternative reasonable scenarios.

       ERCOT and PowerGEM have identified various modeling assumptions that will be used

in the reliability assessment. In response, as we have done with several previous market design

and reliability discussions at the Commission, TSSA has contracted with PA Consulting Group,

Inc. to run SERVM model scenarios to help identify key drivers and provide additional analysis.

Based on our preliminary evaluation, TSSA has identified critical assumptions that not only could

have a significant impact on the modeling results but also have a large cone of uncertainty

associated with them. These four key assumptions are: (1) the demand forecast; (2) the resource

mix; (3) the weighting of historical weather year probabilities; and (4) coal and natural gas prices.

Variations in these inputs can lead to significant changes in the model outcomes. Therefore, TSSA

recommends that the Commission direct ERCOT to model sensitivities for each of these critical

assumptions, in addition to the base case assumptions as recommended by TSSA in these

comments.



                                                 2
        Finally, TSSA recommends that the Commission should update CONE and run sensitivity

analysis using various CONE values. Similar to TSSA concerns regarding the use of uncertain

modeling assumptions that extend several years into the future, the CONE values should also be

run using various sensitivities to give the Commission more data when evaluating potential costs

of various market design proposals. TSSA further discusses its recommended sensitivity scenarios

in response to the Staff’s specific questions.

                                II. RESPONSE TO QUESTIONS

1) At the July 25, 2024 Open Meeting, the Commission approved setting the CONE at

   $140,000/MW-year for planning purposes in the ERCOT region, including the triennial

   reliability assessment. Based on stakeholder feedback, ERCOT has proposed a plan for

   updating this CONE value.

       a. Does CONE need to be updated for the 2026 reliability standard assessment? Why

           or why not?

       TSSA recommends that the Commission update the ERCOT Cost of New Entry (CONE)

values. Because the CONE values will be used by the Commission in evaluating the cost impact

of proposed market design solution options, the CONE value should reflect updated costs so that

the Commission’s evaluation will incorporate realistic cost benchmarks. It is important, therefore,

that the CONE study include appropriate reference technologies using the most up-to-date

information.

       The costs associated with new generation resources are undergoing rapid changes, as are

the options available for procuring essential equipment such as gas turbines and battery

components. New suppliers are entering the market for gas turbine equipment, and it is crucial to

evaluate both the scalability of these alternatives and the feasibility of securing them by the 2029



                                                 3
 operational timeframe to identify the most suitable reference technology and its installed cost. For

example, FTAI Aviation and Boom Supersonic have recently announced increased production of

refurbished jet engines intended for natural gas power generation.1 Additionally, Engineering,

Procurement, and Construction (EPC) costs for generating assets are also continuing to change,

which in turn affects the Cost of New Entry (CONE) for new generation and storage projects.

These rapid changes could make following a traditional CONE estimation procedure more

difficult, so we encourage ERCOT to clearly document their methodology, data sources, and

assumptions publicly for this update.

           Given the uncertainty associated with the rapid evolution in costs and suppliers for new

generation and energy storage resources and the extended timeframe over which the Commission

must evaluate whether the bulk power system is meeting the reliability standard, TSSA

recommends that the Commission direct ERCOT to perform sensitivities over a range of CONE

values when evaluating potential market design changes.

           b. If the Commission considers an updated CONE value, are the scope and list of

               tasks proposed by Brattle and Sargent & Lundy in ERCOT's January 15, 2026

               filing an acceptable method to update the calculations? If not, please provide

               recommended modifications to their approach.

           TSSA offers two recommendations to the Brattle Group (Brattle) and Sargent & Lundy’s

proposed scope and list of tasks. First, TSSA recommends that Brattle add a task to include the

latest cost estimates for Texas Energy Fund (TEF) generators (including those generators that have

withdrawn their applications but still intend to build) be included in the CONE study. These

projects represent some of the most up-to-date actual projects in ERCOT, the Commission has



1
    See Wall Street Journal, “How Jet Engines Are Powering Data Centers,” (February 17, 2026).

                                                          4
 access to these cost estimates, and these costs should be included in the study. TEF projects that

were cancelled due to turbine availability may have also been canceled due to costs, so canceled

projects should also be evaluated. Second, TSSA recommends that Brattle should address and

provide additional details and analysis on the issues previously identified by stakeholders and the

Commission during the development of CONE values for the 2024 CONE Study.2 Specific issues

previously identified included the selection of technology choice (Frame CT versus aero-derivative

CT) and the use of a system-side cost adjustment versus the Houston-centric costs that were

previously estimated by Brattle.

        Finally, ERCOT seeks comment on the inclusion of alternative technology choices. TSSA

supports the assessment of alternative technologies (such as a solar/BESS hybrid or long-duration

stand-alone BESS) for inclusion in the CONE study. The reference technologies should reflect the

near-term investment landscape in ERCOT and represent the types of projects included in the

ERCOT queue expected to be completed during the study period. As such, TSSA recommends

inclusion of additional technology candidates.

2) ERCOT has requested the Commission consider whether the load forecasts used in this

    study should align with the one that will be generated through the 2026 RTP compliance

    plan described in the Commission's rulemaking in Project No. 58480.3 ERCOT

    acknowledges that an updated load forecast that aligns with that compliance plan could

    be ready by April or May 2026, which would push back the timeline of the reliability

    assessment by at least a month.




2
  PUCT Project No. 54584, Reliability Standard for the ERCOT Market, Brattle CONE Study Report and Model
(July 18, 2024).
3
 Project No, 58480, Rulemaking to Establish Large Load Forecasting Criteria under PURA §37.0561, ERCOT’s
Comments Regarding Proposed 16 TAC §25.370 at 6 (October 17, 2025).

                                                     5
        a. Should the Commission approve updating the load forecast used in the 2026

           reliability assessment to align with the compliance plan being considered in

           Project No. 58480, even if it will delay work on the reliability assessment?

       Yes, TSSA recommends that ERCOT update the load forecast to align with the Compliance

Plan for the 2026 RTP in Project No. 58480 to ensure that the most up-to-date validated, load

information is included in the reliability assessment. As previously noted, the load forecast is a

critical input into the model that can have significant impact on the modeling results. It is

imperative that the reliability assessment use the most recent data to support the load forecast. A

one or even two month-delay should be of no concern given the importance and potential market

impacts of this exercise.

       The use of outdated load forecasts could significantly impact the modeling outcomes and

lead to an inaccurate conclusion regarding whether and to what degree the bulk power system is

meeting the reliability standard. ERCOT’s previous legacy forecast method for long-term load

planning and the CDR Report overestimated load growth by including potentially speculative and

duplicative large-load projects without accounting for essential project milestones like site control

and financial commitment.

       The Commission has adopted new rule 16 TAC §25.370, which makes large load

forecasting more accurate. Now, only large loads that have signed interconnection agreements

meeting specific requirements for disclosure, site control, and financial commitment can be

included in ERCOT’s planning and reliability forecasts. This change helps ensure that planning

processes include only viable projects with a demonstrated commercial commitment resulting in

a more accurate forecast. The 2026 Compliance Plan incorporates substantiated load validation

and mitigates these concerns of using an outdated and unsubstantiated legacy load forecast and



                                                 6
 results in a more realistic forecast of load growth that should be included in the reliability

assessment.

       The Commission should not use the previous load forecast in the reliability assessment

because it lacks Commission approved standards for validation and readiness and will overstate

demand, misrepresent reliability risks, and weaken the credibility of the reliability assessment’s

outcomes. A brief delay in the schedule so that ERCOT can incorporate the 2026 RTP-compliant

forecast is warranted because accurate, validated data is critical for reliable modeling and for

meeting legislative requirements for ERCOT’s resource adequacy analyses.

       b. What other considerations should the Commission make regarding the load

           forecast used for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years?

       Using load projections aligned with the 2026 RTP Compliance Plan will improve near-term

forecasting, but significant uncertainty remains regarding demand that can realistically be

energized by 2029. This uncertainty is due to the lengthy process required for transmission

upgrades, supply chain issues for equipment, and extended EPC timelines. As seen nationally,

targeted energization dates do not guarantee the supporting infrastructure will be ready. To

accurately assess the reliability of the ERCOT system for 2029, it is critical to exercise additional

scrutiny to derive the TSP plans and projected timelines for transmission and substation builds to

serve the large loads that requested service in 2029, and to adjust these requests to incorporate the

feasibility of timelines for energizing them. Additionally, there is uncertainty how potential

changes to the current allocation method of allocating transmission costs could impact the

reliability assessment.

         To account for these uncertainties, TSSA recommends that ERCOT run additional

sensitivity analyses addressing the uncertainty in two primary variables influencing the 2029 load


                                                 7
 forecast. First, ERCOT should run sensitivities that incorporate both higher and lower load growth

scenarios, including related curtailment capacities, to determine their effect on reliability metrics.

       Second, ERCOT should assess the impact of potential changes in transmission cost

allocation methods (that transition from the 4CP method to alternatives such as a 12 CP or NCP

methods) on load shapes. Currently, ERCOT’s Large Flexible Load (LFL) hourly load profiles

reflect notable summer afternoon load reductions by LFLs from June through September.

However, the use of different allocation methods would create different incentives for LFLs to

shift consumption, thereby influencing reliability assessments. These potential changes should be

included in ERCOT’s analysis.

       More obviously, ERCOT has a dynamic wholesale and retail market with expectations that

investors, not ratepayers, will take on risks based on their own best interests. We do not expect

data centers to build new facilities blindly without regard to the availability of power. To the extent

that the load forecast drives resource adequacy concerns, we should remember to expect behavioral

responses from investors on both the supply and demand sides.

3) ERCOT proposed using the December 2025 Capacity, Demand, and Reserves (CDR)

   Report to create the base portfolio for evaluating the bulk power system in 2026 and 2029.

   This includes resource additions and retirements.

       a. Does the generation portfolio in the December 2025 CDR Report adequately

           capture the resource mix in both 2026 and 2029? If not, what additional

           assumptions should be made about resource additions and retirements?

       TSSA recommends that the latest projected capacity from Texas Energy Fund (TEF)

program projects be integrated into the resource mix for 2029, to the extent this capacity differs

from the estimate provided in the December 2025 CDR report. Given the Commission's access to



                                                  8
 the most current information regarding construction progress, ERCOT is well-positioned to offer

a more precise assessment of incremental TEF thermal additions for 2029. Furthermore, ERCOT

should include any projects that have withdrawn their TEF loan applications but have notified the

Commission of their intention to proceed independently with a targeted commercial operation date

(COD) of 2029 or earlier.

       TSSA further recommends that ERCOT conduct a sensitivity analysis to evaluate

alternative resource mixes for the study year 2029 that include additional queue capacity that does

not yet meet the planning guide criteria for inclusion in the CDR report but may progress in the

next several years to become a firm supply resource. ERCOT could provide a reasonable estimate

of such capacity by applying a historical success rate to the currently excluded queue capacity to

determine the amount of capacity to include in the analysis.

       Historically, the CDR has never been used to make resource adequacy decisions directly.

Stakeholders and the Commission have recognized it is a useful gauge, but not a precise

measurement. TSSA cautions that this be remembered when making any policy recommendations

based on this tool.

4) Based on information provided by the transmission operators, ERCOT proposed using

   13,988 MW as the magnitude criterion of the reliability standard for the 2026 simulation

   year. For the 2029 simulation year, ERCOT proposes scaling the 2026 magnitude value

   by the ratio of the 75th percentile load forecast for 2029 to the 75th percentile load

   forecast for 2026, resulting in a magnitude value of 14,509 MW for the 2029 simulation

   year.




                                                9
         a. Should the Commission use these values for the magnitude criterion in the 2026

            and 2029 simulation years? If not, what modifications to these values should be

            made?

        TSSA recommends that the peak demand estimates for determining the magnitude criterion

exclude the large loads for the 2026 and 2029 study years and that SB 6 large load curtailment not

be treated as a load shed event. It does appear that ERCOT’s calculation of the Adjusted Load

Forecast for Winter 2025-2026 for Reliability Standard Magnitude excludes these large loads from

the peak demand value of 77,338 MW, which is used in the magnitude calculation.4 However,

ERCOT should clarify how these large loads are treated when applying the magnitude threshold.

It is not clear if curtailing these large loads, which happens prior to rotating load shed by TSPs,

would count against the proposed 13,988 MW magnitude criterion that ERCOT determined for

2026, and the 14,509 MW criterion that ERCOT determined for 2029.

        ERCOT states in its assumptions (and in the CDR assumptions) that it assumes all data

centers and 85 percent of industrial, hydrogen, and cryptocurrency loads are curtailable under SB6

implementation criteria. ERCOT also states that the magnitude criteria are derived from the peak

demand estimates without including large loads for the 2026 and 2029 study years. As the CDR

reserve margin analysis shows, including the SB6 large load curtailment capacity as a resource

prior to rotating load shed for other customers increases the system reserve margins for 2029 from

a negative 5.8% to a positive 28.9%. This appropriately indicates a healthier system with lower

likelihood of rotating outages by TSPs to the rest of the (non-large load) customers.




4
 ERCOT’s Adjusted Load Forecast for Winter 2025-1016 for the Reliability Standard Magnitude can be accessed at
https://www.ercot.com/gridinfo/load/forecast.


                                                     10
        Consistent with ERCOT’s modeling simulations that use large load curtailment to maintain

reliability and prevent rotating outages for other customers, these curtailed MW should not be

classified as load shed events. Therefore, TSSA recommends that reliability metrics (frequency,

duration, magnitude) should only include load shed MW from non-large load customers, excluding

large load curtailments.

5) ERCOT proposed using the EIA' s 2025 Annual Energy Outlook and EIA Form 923 data

   to determine the natural gas and coal prices for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years. This

   results in prices of $2.84/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.47/MMBtu for coal in 2026 and

   $3.16/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.41/MMBtu for coal in 2029.

       a. Are these assumptions for fuel prices for the 2026/2029 simulation years

           reasonable? If not, what alternative sources of information should be considered

           to determine these fuels prices?

       ERCOT’s assumptions for natural gas and coal prices seem low compared to current market

fundamentals. Underestimating fuel costs in the SERVM modeling could result in inaccuracies in

the reliability assessment outcomes by undervaluing certain resources and inappropriately

modeling ESR behavior. Fuel price assumptions influence unit dispatch, market prices, and may

cause the model to undervalue resources like price-responsive demand if proposed gas prices are

set lower than expected. Fuel costs also affect ESR charging and discharging costs and predicted

ESR energy levels during peak demand, which impact reliability metrics and simulation results.

       TSSA recommends that ERCOT use traded forward market prices from representative

trading hubs instead of EIA data for more accurate, liquid, and transparent fuel price assumptions.

With rising gas demand from factors like increased LNG exports and expanding gas-fired

generation to meet increasing demand, forward market prices better reflect market views for 2026


                                                11
 and 2029. For instance, settled gas forwards for the Houston Ship Channel show a $4.3/MMBtu

expectation for 2026, compared to ERCOT's proposed $2.84/MMBtu. TSSA recommends using

recent market forwards and representative trading hubs to determine the market forward curve for

natural gas and coal inputs for use in the modeling.

       TSSA also recommends using weather year daily gas price modeling to capture gas price

variance in the weather year simulations, as extreme weather events are associated with volatility

in the gas markets. ERCOT proposes to use the monthly average shape of Henry Hub in recent

history to derive monthly gas prices from the EIA-projected annual gas prices. However, this does

not reflect gas price correlation with extreme weather on a daily basis. ERCOT should generate

historical daily gas price to monthly average gas price ratios for past weather years and incorporate

these shapes in gas price inputs to better capture the thermal supply curve during these events.

       b. Should any sensitivity analyses on these fuel prices be considered?

       TSSA recommends that ERCOT run sensitivity analysis on fuel prices using high and low

assumptions from market forward prices. Because fuel prices significantly affect dispatch order,

market prices, and resource availability, including a +/- 20% range around the base case

assumptions helps capture potential operational and market impacts. Natural gas prices can be

volatile during extreme weather, affecting both demand response and ESR behavior. Natural gas

prices, in particular, are highly sensitive to expectations of extreme cold weather, and periods of

elevated gas prices can increase the responsiveness of industrial load, on‑site generation, and other

demand‑side resources, thereby reducing net demand during high‑risk events. Higher gas and

power prices also materially affect the charging and discharging patterns of ESR resources, which

can alter their availability during energy‑constrained conditions. Factoring in these sensitivities

ensures a more accurate risk assessment under different fuel-cost scenarios.



                                                 12
 6) For previous reliability assessments, ERCOT has treated all historical weather years as

   having equal probability. For this assessment, ERCOT proposed weighing recent years

   more heavily.

        a. Should the Commission consider not treating all historical weather years as

           having equal probability? If yes, do you agree with ERCOT' s proposed weighting

           of weather years?

        b. If you have an alternative weighting methodology, please provide additional

           details on your proposal. Please include justification for why your approach is

           better than what ERCOT has proposed.

       TSSA does not support ERCOT’s proposed weather-year weighting methodology due to a

lack of rigorous statistical analysis to ensure that extreme outlier years are not over‑represented in

the reliability results. The weather year weighting methodology is one of the key modeling

variables that greatly impacts the modeling results and, therefore, the weather weighting

assumptions must be grounded in sound science and supported by data to ensure that the reliability

assessment modeling outcomes are credible. ERCOT’s intent to more accurately capture weather

trends is reasonable, and we appreciate the effort, but ERCOT’s proposed methodology does not

incorporate the type of robust probabilistic or climatological methods needed to determine whether

(or which) recent years should receive a higher weight, and if so the proper weighting. As

reliability risk in ERCOT is highly sensitive to the frequency and severity of extreme cold events,

an appropriate weighting framework should be developed in consultation with meteorologists and

climate experts who can assess the likelihood of these events going forward. The use of a

statistically defensible, expert‑informed probabilistic methodology that properly balances climate

trends with outlier control could be a reasonable approach, but that is not the method proposed by



                                                 13
 ERCOT at this time. Therefore, TSSA recommends that ERCOT’s proposed weather year

weighting approach be rejected.

       If there is insufficient time to develop a statistically defensible probabilistic method based

upon expert statistical analysis, TSSA recommends that ERCOT perform sensitivity analysis.

TSSA supports an approach that recognizes the low likelihood of extreme weather-years.

However, ERCOT’s proposed methodology to linearly increase weights annually from 1980

through 2023 based on trends in cooling degree days and heating degree days appears to be an

arbitrary approach.

       To understand the impact of ERCOT’s proposed methodology and to avoid overreliance

on this method, TSSA recommends running multiple scenarios to provide a range of outcomes

associated with the Weather Year Weighting modeling input that includes, at a minimum:

       •   An assessment of only more recent weather years with equal weighting (e.g., only the

           last 15 weather years, instead of going back to 1980).

       •   An approach that uses equal weights for all 44 weather years.

These sensitivity analysis scenarios combined with the base case recency weighted approach

proposed by ERCOT will provide the Commission and the public an informed view on the impact

of this modeling choice.

7) ERCOT proposed using the multi-area reliability and economic dispatch modeling

   capability in SERVM to assess resource adequacy on a zonal basis that would account for

   transmission constraints between defined transmission zones. ERCOT states that any

   results from this analysis would be informational and not used to determine compliance

   with the reliability standard.




                                                14
           a. Should the Commission approve an assessment of reliability metrics at the zonal

              level, understanding that these results would be purely informational and not used

              to determine compliance with the reliability standard?

         No. TSSA recommends that ERCOT should not include informational zonal reliability

metrics at this time as this approach needs more refinement to provide reliable and credible results.5

The inclusion of the zonal modeling could lead to confusion by the public and reliance unreliable

conclusions. ERCOT’s own transmission-modeling discussion indicates that the current zonal

representation requires substantial additional refinement, noting that early tests show significantly

different result, including much higher LOLE, relative to the recommended single-zone “copper

sheet” model. The zonal methodology needs further development before it can reliably represent

emergency transfers or be used to assess reliability outcomes.6 7

          Introducing zonal metrics that are known to be unreliable and highly sensitive risks

distracting from the central question in this effort of whether ERCOT meets the reliability standard.

Further, it may lead to misinterpretation of preliminary, non-robust results and arguments for

market design changes despite the intended informational nature of the exercise. For these reasons,

TSSA recommends that ERCOT continue to work on refining the zonal model for discussion at

                                                            15
 SAWG, but not include zonal modeling, even as a sensitivity, in the reliability assessment at this

time.

        b. If so, do you have any proposed modifications to the approach ERCOT has

           recommended?

        ERCOT and PowerGEM’s resources are better spent modeling the sensitivity scenarios that

TSSA recommends for the variables and inputs that have significant impact on the probabilistic

reliability assessment rather than to move forward on an experimental approach that has yet to be

fully developed by ERCOT or vetted by stakeholders.

8) ERCOT proposed modifying how the model accounts for the effectiveness of the

   Commission's weatherization rule 16 TAC § 25.55. Previously, it was estimated to reduce

   weather-related outages by 85%, however under ERCOT' s proposed approach, the

   rule's effectiveness would decline during extreme temperatures.

    a. Do you agree with ERCOT's recommendation to deviate from the 85% effectiveness

        for the weatherization rule?

        TSSA agrees with ERCOT’s recommendation to deviate from the 85% weatherization

effectiveness assumption in the reliability assessment. ERCOT’s updated methodology is an

improvement over the previous approach because it captures both the expected performance gains

from weatherization and the remaining outage risk during extreme cold conditions. For future

assessments, ERCOT should continue to refine this assumption as empirical performance data

becomes available from winter operations, allowing the model to incorporate observed outcomes

and ensure the weatherization effectiveness factor remains well‑supported and realistic.




                                               16
 9) ERCOT has proposed assumptions for the outages.

        a. Are the assumptions for generation and ESR outage modeling reasonable? If not,

            what modifications do you propose?

        b. How should ERCOT treat planned transmission outages in the model?

        TSSA does not recommend multi-area zonal modeling for informational purposes in this

proceeding (see TSSA Response to Question 7). For the system level reliability modeling, TSSA

recommends not including transmission outages to reflect generation availability or load

deliverability to contain the scope of this effort.

10)   Please provide comments and recommendations on any of the model input
assumptions that Staff has not specifically flagged in previous questions.
        TSSA respectfully recommends that ERCOT offer greater transparency regarding two key

model inputs: (1) ESR Representation and (2) Price Responsive Demand (PRD) and the 4-

Coincident Peak (4CP) Program. Specifically, ERCOT should be required to disclose its modeling

assumptions regarding the ESR fleet.

        According to ERCOT, SERVM will be configured to manage State of Charge (SOC) based

on economic optimization, rather than reliability-based optimization. Two primary parameters

influencing ESR output and reserves in the model are cycling limits and Round-Trip Efficiency

assumptions for the ESR fleet. To enhance stakeholder understanding of the modeling, ERCOT

should publish detailed assumptions about the ESR fleet, including the distribution of durations

(e.g., 1-hour, 2-hour, and 4-hour ESRs), any imposed daily or annual cycling limits, and the

presumed round-trip efficiency. This information will also enable stakeholders to conduct their

own modeling analyses with greater accuracy.

        Second, regarding the PRD and 4CP modelling input, TSSA recommends that ERCOT

include additional PRD reductions from growth in distributed generation, particularly natural gas

                                                  17
 distributed generation, which is not already captured from the growth of LFLs. ERCOT states that

the load reduction impacts of PRD (including standalone LFLs) and 4 CP load reductions are

already embedded in the weather-year load forecasts. This appears to assume that the growth in

PRD is resulting only from the growth in LFLs that ERCOT projects in its load forecast. However,

there is additional distributed generation that should also be included.

         For example, ERCOT’s Annual Distributed Generation Estimate8 shows consistent growth

in thermal distributed generators greater than 1 MW that were estimated to be in the 500 MW –

600 MW range in 2024. This capacity is likely expected to continue to grow through 2029, and it

is expected that these generators will operate to protect host loads from scarcity pricing in the

market. Demand responsive customer load sometimes requires capital and O&M – similar to a

generator. To the extent ERCOT’s projections for PRD do not capture growth in DG, particularly,

gas and diesel fired DG, TSSA recommends ERCOT incorporate additional price responsive

demand capacity in its resource mix for inclusion in the model.

                                               III. CONCLUSION

         TSSA appreciates the opportunity to provide feedback on the modeling assumptions and

additional sensitivity analysis that should be included in the reliability assessment. We look

forward to continuing to work with Staff, ERCOT, and other stakeholders on these issues.

                                                                 Respectfully submitted

                                                                 _____________________

                                                                 Mark R. Stover
                                                                 Executive Director
                                                                 Texas Solar + Storage Association
                                                                 P.O. Box 1485
                                                                 Austin, Texas 78767
                                                                 Marks@txsolarstorage.org

                                    PROJECT NO. 58777

TRIENNIAL RELIABILITY                           §     PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
ASSESSMENT FOR THE ERCOT                        §
REGION UNDER §25.508                            §                  OF TEXAS

             TEXAS SOLAR + STORAGE ASSOCIATION COMMENTS
                         EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 •   The results of the reliability assessment are largely dependent upon the assumptions and
     forecasts used in the model, many of which have significant uncertainty, particularly for
     the 2029 study year. The Commission carefully consider and evaluate multiple scenarios

       The Texas Solar + Storage Association files these comments in response to the questions

filed by the Staff of the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Staff) in this project on January 30,

       The Texas Solar + Storage Association (TSSA) is the statewide association dedicated to

the expansion of solar power and energy storage technologies in Texas. Our member companies

are engaged in the development, installation, and operations of utility-scale, industrial,

commercial, and residential solar and energy storage facilities and products, serving wholesale and

retail customers with predictable, affordable, clean power. Since 2014, TSSA has advocated on

behalf ofits members before the Texas Legislature, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT

or Commission), as well as ERCOT. Our members have installed roughly two-thirds of the solar

                                 I.   GENERAL COMMENTS

       TSSA appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the inputs and assumptions

proposed by ERCOT for use in the probabilistic reliability assessment required by 16 TAC

§25.508(c). The results of this reliability assessment are largely dependent upon the assumptions

and forecasts used in the model, many of which have significant uncertainty, particularly for the

2029 study year. If the assessment demonstrates that the ERCOT market is not meeting the

reliability standard, the Commission will consider market design changes that could potentially


                                                 1
 improve the reliability of ERCOT bulk power system based upon these assessment results. Given

the great uncertainty associated with some of the modeling assumptions, as well as the resulting

costs on customers and market impacts ofany potential market design changes, TSSArecommends

that the Commission carefully consider and evaluate multiple scenarios and sensitivities associated

with key reliability assessment assumptions, particularly for the 2029 study year. The Commission

could then consider the costs of various proposals to meet any identified deficiency under a base

case scenario, as well as under sensitivity cases. This will help inform the Commission and the

public when weighing the potential costs and benefits associated with any market design changes,

if needed. Requiring ERCOT to run sensitivity analyses in addition to the base case recognizes

that the modeling results are dependent upon highly uncertain inputs and have a range of outcomes

that could occur under alternative reasonable scenarios.

       ERCOT and PowerGEM have identified various modeling assumptions that will be used

in the reliability assessment.   In response, as we have done with several previous market design

and reliability discussions at the Commission, TSSA has contracted with PA Consulting Group,

Inc. to run SERVM model scenarios to help identify key drivers and provide additional analysis.

Based on our preliminary evaluation, TSSA has identified critical assumptions that not only could

have a significant impact on the modeling results but also have a large cone of uncertainty

associated with them. These four key assumptions are: (1) the demand forecast; (2) the resource

mix; (3) the weighting of historical weather year probabilities; and (4) coal and natural gas prices.

Variations in these inputs can lead to significant changes in the model outcomes. Therefore, TSSA

recommends that the Commission direct ERCOT to model sensitivities for each of these critical

assumptions, in addition to the base case assumptions as recommended by TSSA in these

comments.

lead to an inaccurate conclusion regarding whether and to what degree the bulk power system is

meeting the reliability standard. ERCOT's previous legacy forecast method for long-term load

planning and the CDR Report overestimated load growth by including potentially speculative and

duplicative large-load projects without accounting for essential project milestones like site control

and financial commitment.

forecasting more accurate. Now, only large loads that have signed interconnection agreements

meeting specific requirements for disclosure, site control, and financial commitment can be

included in ERCOT's planning and reliability forecasts. This change helps ensure that planning

processes include only viable proj ects with a demonstrated commercial commitment resulting in

a more accurate forecast. The 2026 Compliance Plan incorporates substantiated load validation

and mitigates these concerns of using an outdated and unsubstantiated legacy load forecast and

assessment.

because it lacks Commission approved standards for validation and readiness and will overstate

demand, misrepresent reliability risks, and weaken the credibility of the reliability assessment's

outcomes. A brief delay in the schedule so that ERCOT can incorporate the 2026 RTP-compliant

forecast is warranted because accurate, validated data is critical for reliable modeling and for

meeting legislative requirements for ERCOT's resource adequacy analyses.

5) ERCOT proposed using the EIA' s 2025 Annual Energy Outlook and EIA Form 923 data

   to determine the natural gas and coal prices for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years. This

   results in prices of $2.84/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.47/MMBtu for coal in 2026 and

       a. Are these assumptions for fuel prices for the 2026/2029 simulation years

           reasonable? If not, what alternative sources of information should be considered

           to determine these fuels prices?

       ERCOT's assumptions for natural gas and coal prices seem low compared to current market

fundamentals. Underestimating fuel costs in the SERVM modeling could result in inaccuracies in

the reliability assessment outcomes by undervaluing certain resources and inappropriately

modeling ESR behavior. Fuel price assumptions influence unit dispatch, market prices, and may

cause the model to undervalue resources like price-responsive demand if proposed gas prices are

set lower than expected. Fuel costs also affect ESR charging and discharging costs and predicted

ESR energy levels during peak demand, which impact reliability metrics and simulation results.

       TSSA recommends that ERCOT use traded forward market prices from representative

trading hubs instead of EIA data for more accurate, liquid, and transparent fuel price assumptions.

With rising gas demand from factors like increased LNG exports and expanding gas-fired

generation to meet increasing demand, forward market prices better reflect market views for 2026


                                                11
 and 2029. For instance, settled gas forwards for the Houston Ship Channel show a $4.3/MMBtu

expectation for 2026, compared to ERCOT's proposed $2.84/MMBtu. TSSA recommends using

recent market forwards and representative trading hubs to determine the market forward curve for

natural gas and coal inputs for use in the modeling.

       TSSA also recommends using weather year daily gas price modeling to capture gas price

variance in the weather year simulations, as extreme weather events are associated with volatility

in the gas markets. ERCOT proposes to use the monthly average shape of Henry Hub in recent

history to derive monthly gas prices from the EIA-projected annual gas prices. However, this does

not reflect gas price correlation with extreme weather on a daily basis. ERCOT should generate

historical daily gas price to monthly average gas price ratios for past weather years and incorporate

these shapes in gas price inputs to better capture the thermal supply curve during these events.

       b. Should any sensitivity analyses on these fuel prices be considered?

       TSSA recommends that ERCOT run sensitivity analysis on fuel prices using high and low

assumptions from market forward prices. Because fuel prices significantly affect dispatch order,

market prices, and resource availability, including a +/- 20% range around the base case

assumptions helps capture potential operational and market impacts. Natural gas prices can be

volatile during extreme weather, affecting both demand response and ESR behavior. Natural gas

prices, in particular, are highly sensitive to expectations of extreme cold weather, and periods of

elevated gas prices can increase the responsiveness of industrial load, on-site generation, and other

demand-side resources, thereby reducing net demand during high-risk events. Higher gas and

power prices also materially affect the charging and discharging patterns of ESR resources, which

can alter their availability during energy-constrained conditions. Factoring in these sensitivities

ensures a more accurate risk assessment under different fuel-cost scenarios.

variables that greatly impacts the modeling results and, therefore, the weather weighting

assumptions must be grounded in sound science and supported by data to ensure that the reliability

assessment modeling outcomes are credible. ERCOT's intent to more accurately capture weather

trends is reasonable, and we appreciate the effort, but ERCOT's proposed methodology does not

incorporate the type of robust probabilistic or climatological methods needed to determine whether

(or which) recent years should receive a higher weight, and if so the proper weighting. As

reliability risk in ERCOT is highly sensitive to the frequency and severity of extreme cold events,

an appropriate weighting framework should be developed in consultation with meteorologists and

climate experts who can assess the likelihood of these events going forward.           The use of a

improvement over the previous approach because it captures both the expected performance gains

from weatherization and the remaining outage risk during extreme cold conditions. For future

assessments, ERCOT should continue to refine this assumption as empirical performance data

becomes available from winter operations, allowing the model to incorporate observed outcomes

and ensure the weatherization effectiveness factor remains well-supported and realistic.

10)     Please provide comments and recommendations on any of the model input
assumptions that Staff has not specifically ilagged in previous questions.

        TSSA respectfully recommends that ERCOT offer greater transparency regarding two key

model inputs: (1) ESR Representation and (2) Price Responsive Demand (PRD) and the 4-

Coincident Peak (4CP) Program. Specifically, ERCOT should be required to disclose its modeling

assumptions regarding the ESR fleet.

        According to ERCOT, SERVM will be configured to manage State of Charge (SOC) based

on economic optimization, rather than reliability-based optimization. Two primary parameters

influencing ESR output and reserves in the model are cycling limits and Round-Trip Efficiency

assumptions for the ESR fleet. To enhance stakeholder understanding of the modeling, ERCOT

should publish detailed assumptions about the ESR fleet, including the distribution of durations

(e.g., 1-hour, 2-hour, and 4-hour ESRs), any imposed daily or annual cycling limits, and the

presumed round-trip efficiency. This information will also enable stakeholders to conduct their

own modeling analyses with greater accuracy.

        Second, regarding the PRI) and 4CP modelling input, TSSA recommends that ERCOT

include additional PRI reductions from growth in distributed generation, particularly natural gas

PRD is resulting only from the growth in LFLs that ERCOT proj ects in its load forecast. However,

there is additional distributed generation that should also be included.

         For example, ERCOT's Annual Distributed Generation Estimatex shows consistent growth

in thermal distributed generators greater than 1 MW that were estimated to be in the 500 MW -

600 MW range in 2024. This capacity is likely expected to continue to grow through 2029, and it

is expected that these generators will operate to protect host loads from scarcity pricing in the

gas and diesel fired DG, TSSA recommends ERCOT incorporate additional price responsive

demand capacity in its resource mix for inclusion in the model.

Consistent with ERCOT's modeling simulations that use large load curtailment to maintain
reliability and prevent rotating outages for other customers, these curtailed MW should not
be classified as load shed events. Reliability metrics (frequency, duration, magnitude)
should include only load shed MW from non-large load customers, excluding large load
curtailments.
ERCOT use traded forward market prices from representative trading hubs instead of EIA
data for more accurate, liquid, and transparent fuel price assumptions. ERCOT should use
weather year daily gas price modeling to capture gas price variance in the weather year
simulations, as extreme weather events are associated with volatility in the gas markets.
ERCOT should run sensitivity analysis on fuel prices using high and low assumptions from
market forward prices.
ERCOT's proposed weather year weighting approach should not be included in the model
due to a lack of rigorous statistical analysis that ensures that extreme outlier years are not
over-represented in the reliability results. Instead, if the Commission desires to use a
different weighting methodology, ERCOT should develop a statistically defensible,
expert-informed probabilistic methodology that properly balances climate trends with
outlier control. Alternatively, ERCOT should run sensitivity analysis on the weather year
weighting modeling input that includes, at a minimum: 1) An assessment of only more
recent weather years with equal weighting (e.g., only the last 15 weather years, instead of
going back to 1980); and 2) an approach that uses equal weights for all 44 weather years.
ERCOT should not include informational zonal reliability metrics at this time as this
approach needs more refinement to provide reliable and credible results.
